args.summary: Woman in her early 30s with a continent urinary pouch. Catheterizing had been getting harder for weeks, so an indwelling pouch catheter was placed. It stopped draining the night before presentation and urine output fell. She then developed severe lower abdominal pain and worsening shortness of breath, and she was in cardiopulmonary decompensation on arrival. WBC is 15.3 and platelets 513. Creatinine is 1.08 mg/dL, eGFR 68 and CRP 1.7. Urgent CT with contrast instilled into the pouch shows a large left laterodorsal defect in the reservoir, with contrast leaking into the peritoneum and free fluid in the abdomen. This fits intraperitoneal rupture of the pouch with urinary peritonitis. The dyspnea is likely from abdominal distension, diaphragmatic splinting and possible early sepsis.
working_diagnoses: Intraperitoneal rupture of continent urinary reservoir (pouch perforation) with urinary ascites/urinary peritonitis
Early sepsis / systemic inflammatory response from urinary peritonitis
Respiratory compromise secondary to abdominal distension/diaphragmatic splinting
Chronic pouch outlet or catheterization dysfunction (e.g., stenosis of the catheterizable channel) as the underlying cause
Rule out concurrent bowel injury or ischemia
next_actions: Resuscitate with oxygen, IV access and a balanced crystalloid bolus
Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam) after taking blood cultures and a culture of pouch urine
Decompress the pouch and drain the peritoneum as a temporary measure if feasible
Emergent laparotomy with pouch repair and peritoneal lavage

provider_metadata.assistant_note: Disposition: ICU admission after emergency laparotomy and repair of the ruptured continent urinary pouch.

args.rationale: She arrived in cardiopulmonary decompensation (physical_exam_004). CT showed urinary peritonitis from intraperitoneal rupture of the continent pouch: a large left laterodorsal defect with contrast leak and free fluid (imaging_005). WBC was 15.3 (lab_007). Emergency laparotomy confirmed the rupture and repaired it; the pouch catheter was secured and a nasogastric tube placed (procedure_result_012). She needs ICU monitoring for sepsis, respiratory support, fluid balance and ileus.
args.followup_or_handoff: ICU handoff: 1) Keep the pouch catheter fixed on free drainage and flush it gently at low volume as the surgeons direct; do not remove or replace it without urology. 2) Keep the nasogastric tube on free drainage, keep her nil by mouth and watch for ileus. 3) Continue IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours. Allergy status was not reported, so confirm there is no beta-lactam allergy before the next dose. Take blood and pouch urine cultures if not already done and tailor antibiotics to the results. 4) Track urine output hourly and check creatinine, electrolytes, bicarbonate (risk of hyperchloremic acidosis with a bowel reservoir), lactate, CBC and CRP every day. 5) Give VTE prophylaxis once surgical bleeding risk allows. 6) Before removing the catheter, check the pouch for leaks with a contrast study (pouchogram), usually at about 2–3 weeks. 7) Urology to find the cause of the catheterization difficulty (e.g., stenosis of the catheterizable channel or pouch outlet) and plan a long-term drainage strategy. Teach the patient to recognize catheter blockage and to get urgent care if drainage stops.
